Engine loads; test started around 12:15, we see a slowly increasing CPU load and a slowly increasing memory consumption due to the number of active process instances in memory. Due to the the compact in-memory representation of process instance state memory consumption is relatively small.

Kafka:

It seems that we reached the part where the engine nodes becomes the bottleneck. At a certain point Kafka cpu usage does not increase anymore. So probably by adding another engine node we could have even scaled up further.

Conclusion

In this sustained benchmark with a “typical” BPMN process (10 service tasks, 200 ms each, 2 timers of 1 minute), TaktX demonstrated both high throughput and stable latency at scale.

With one engine node, throughput plateaued around 850 PI/s (~12k flow nodes/s) while sustaining over 100,000 concurrent active processes with sub-second latency (p95 ~400–500 ms).

With two engine nodes, throughput scaled nearly linearly to ~1,700 PI/s (~24k flow nodes/s) with over 200,000 concurrent processes — without any meaningful increase in latency.

Process durations tracked the theoretical 122 s baseline, confirming timers and workers were correctly orchestrated under load.

These results highlight that TaktX is not only capable of extreme raw throughput (as shown in Scenario 1), but also delivers predictable, real-world sustained performance with millions of concurrent long-running process instances — while maintaining linear scalability across nodes.
